data.content_ref: inline:SRC_004's countercondition—that a structural intervention establishing a causal link would make the distinction ontological—contradicts the main claim that the distinction is purely epistemological. If even a single successful structural intervention can conclusively demonstrate an ontological causal link, then the distinction is not 'always' epistemological; it becomes ontological whenever the intervention succeeds. This means the foundation artifacts are internally inconsistent: they cannot simultaneously assert that independence is always a revisable epistemic hypothesis and that there exists an experimental procedure (structural intervention) that can settle the matter definitively. It is refuted if the structural intervention's 'conclusive' demonstration is shown to depend on background assumptions that remain epistemically revisable, preserving the epistemological primacy.
